record.paper_title: Geodesic Nets: Some Examples and Open Problems
record.original_question: For each positive integer n, does there exist a function f(n) such that every finite connected geodesic multinet in R^2 with exactly three boundary or unbalanced vertices, no edge joining two unbalanced vertices, all balanced vertices of degree at least 3, and every edge carrying positive integer multiplicity at most n, has at most f(n) balanced vertices?

evidence.quote: Geodesic multinets are defined in the same way with the two following distinctions: 1) Edges are allowed to intersect and self-intersect; 2) Each edge is endowed with a positive integer multiplicity;

Problem 3.1.4. Is there a function f (n) such that for each geodesic multinet with three boundary vertices in the Euclidean plane such the that multiplicities of all edges do not exceed n the number of balanced vertices does not exceed f (n)?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setup. Work in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$. A geodesic multinet is a finite connected graph embedded in $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose vertices are points of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and whose edges are straight line segments (edges may intersect or self-intersect at points that are not vertices), with each edge $e$ assigned a positive integer multiplicity $m(e)$. The vertices are partitioned into boundary (unbalanced) vertices and balanced vertices, where a vertex $v$ is called balanced if
$$\sum_{e \ni v} m(e)\, u_e(v) \;=\; 0,$$
the sum running over all edges $e$ incident to $v$, with $u_e(v)$ denoting the unit vector at $v$ pointing along $e$ away from $v$ (each loop contributing two such unit vectors). A vertex that is not balanced is called unbalanced (or boundary).

Question. For every positive integer $n$, does there exist a number $f(n)$ with the following property: every finite connected geodesic multinet in $\mathbb{R}^2$ satisfying
(i) exactly three of its vertices are unbalanced,
(ii) no edge joins two unbalanced vertices,
(iii) every balanced vertex has degree at least $3$, and
(iv) the multiplicity $m(e)$ of each edge satisfies $1 \le m(e) \le n$,
has at most $f(n)$ balanced vertices?
artifact.status_search_result: Recent work establishes that ordinary geodesic nets (multiplicity 1) with three boundary vertices in the plane (and even in non-positively curved planes) have at most one balanced vertex, while multinets with three unbalanced vertices and unbounded multiplicities can have arbitrarily many balanced vertices. However, no source located resolves the bounded-multiplicity version asking for an upper bound f(n) depending on the maximum multiplicity n, so the problem appears to remain open, though this could not be definitively verified.

status_evidence.title: On the existence of a balanced vertex in geodesic nets with three boundary vertices
status_evidence.snippet: A geodesic net with three unbalanced vertices on a plane of non-positive curvature has at most one balanced vertex.
status_evidence.claim: The non-multinet, three-boundary case is well understood (at most one balanced vertex), but this does not address the bounded-multiplicity multinet problem.

status_evidence.title: Geodesic nets with three boundary vertices (Parsons, JDG)
status_evidence.snippet: Geodesic nets with three boundary vertices in the Euclidean plane have at most one balanced vertex.
status_evidence.claim: Confirms the resolution of the multiplicity-one case for three boundary vertices.

status_evidence.title: Towards Constructing Geodesic Nets with Four Boundary Vertices
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses unboundedness of balanced vertices for four boundary vertices; references the three-boundary multinet open problem.
status_evidence.claim: Active research continues in adjacent settings; no resolution of the bounded-multiplicity three-boundary multinet question is reported.
